Abu Muawiya the Blind said that al-Amash had told him: “I saw Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla (one of the Murji'ite leaders) when al-Hajjaj had him brought to a standstill and said to him, ‘Curse the liars, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd.’ Abd al-Rahman replied, ‘May God curse the liars.’ Then he began a fresh statement, saying, ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd.’” Al-Amash added: “I realised that he had started a new sentence: the names stood on their own and were not part of the curse.” See Ibn Saad, The Great Biographical Classes (al-Tabaqat al-Kubra), vol. 6, pp. 112–113.

It seems to us that the rapprochement between the Murji'ites and the Shia at that time was temporary, made necessary by their shared aim of opposing the Umayyads. The Shia actually harboured a deep hostility towards the Murji'ites, while the latter adapted their beliefs to suit the circumstances. Nothing illustrates this better than the conduct of one of their leaders, Amir ibn Sharahil al-Shabi. He declared himself a Shia and joined the revolt of al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd al-Thaqafi, then abandoned that position when the revolt failed. He took part in the movement of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ashath, but when that too failed, he declared his repentance before al-Hajjaj, who appointed him judge of Kufa. When the Umayyad state fell, he proclaimed his loyalty to the Abbasids, who kept him in office. A man whose allegiances changed so readily offers evidence of “the opportunism associated with the Murji'ites”. Consider al-Shabi's own words: “Love the righteous among the believers and among the Banu Hashim, but do not become a Shia. Leave judgement on what you do not know for later, but do not become a Murji'ite. Know that good deeds come from God and bad deeds from yourself, but do not become a Qadarite. Love anyone you see doing good, even if he is a man from Sind with a disfigured nose.” See Ibn Saad, vol. 5, p. 245 and following, vol. 6, pp. 248–249. This shows that the Murji'ites “gave their allegiance to whoever prevailed”. ↩

Yazid ibn al-Muhallab had been governor of Iraq under the caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik. He dealt severely with the family of al-Hajjaj al-Thaqafi. Al-Hajjaj's daughter was married to Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik, who resented what Ibn al-Muhallab had done and threatened him, saying, “By God, if I come to hold any power, I will cut off one of your limbs.” Ibn al-Muhallab replied, “By God, if that happens, I will come at you with a hundred swords.” See Ibn al-Athir, vol. 4, p. 151. ↩

Anonymous, Al-Uyun wa al-Hadaiq, p. 65. A poem by the Murji'ite poet Thabit Qutna, secretary to Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, is an important document for understanding the political thinking of the Murji'ites in this period. We quote these lines:

Hind, listen to me: this is the way we live — We worship God and set no other beside Him. When matters are unclear, we leave judgement for later, But speak the truth about those who act unjustly or defy what is right. We shed no blood unless our own blood is sought; Then there is but one open road to bloodshed.
